title: The safety reporting product, module by module
eyebrow: Product design · Ten modules · One design system
description: A product-grade concept for a restaurant safety reporting system, module by module, with every design decision traced to a research finding and checked against a shipped pattern. By Sam Mozaffari.
deck: Ten modules of a safety reporting product for a restaurant network, each screen annotated with the research finding that drove the decision and the alternative it replaced.

facts.dd: Into the live reporting programme in December 2025: the findings report, a five-stage service blueprint, a prioritised three-phase roadmap and the form prototypes, refined through a stakeholder validation session.

Safety items on the network-wide employee engagement survey read across the whole workforce of tens of thousands of team members, then interviews, restaurant visits and two form walkthroughs, held as 232 typed insight records tied to a five-stage blueprint.
Hand-written HTML and CSS on a token-based design system, gated by a contrast script and a site lint. Every component was checked against shipped products on Mobbin before it was drawn.
Vendor, sites and people are removed, and every name and number on these screens is written for the walkthrough.

intro.title: What you are looking at
body: **The problem.** A safety incident and hazard reporting platform, configured for one workflow across several hundred restaurants: a team member notices something, scans the poster, fills in the form. The research found a different workflow in almost every restaurant. The team member tells the manager. The manager decides whether it is worth logging, logs it if so, and sometimes closes it without telling anyone. Reporting volume varied widely between sites and the platform's own data could not say whether a quiet restaurant was safe or silent.

**What the research changed.** The business assumed location explained the difference, so the sample was designed to test that: eight restaurants across high- and low-reporting sites, higher- and lower-crime suburbs, metropolitan and regional. Location did not predict it. The manager did. That finding reorganised the recommendations, and it organises these screens.

**From the findings to the product.** The delivered recommendations changed what the form asks and what managers do, inside a platform the business had already bought. This is the next move: the whole service redrawn as a product, module by module, following the navigation the restaurants already knew. Each module below is one item from that navigation, designed from the evidence.

**How to read a module.** The finding sits above the screen. The screen is shown whole, at full size, with numbered pins. Each pin names the finding, the decision it drove, the alternative it replaced and the shipped product the pattern was checked against. The states that matter sit underneath. [The case study](../index.html) carries the research, the method and what the internal tool saved.

system.title: One set of tokens, one set of components, no framework
body: Every screen here is hand-written HTML on two stylesheets: a token file and a component file. Nothing is generated by a UI kit and nothing is a picture of a component. The tokens below are read out of the live token file when this page is built, so what you see is what the screens use.

The type scale has seven steps from a 14px base. Spacing is a 4px grid. There are three radii and two elevations. Colour is one neutral ramp plus four status pairs, each pair a foreground and a ground; a contrast script checks every text pair at 4.5 to 1 and every border at 3 to 1 before a screen is captured, and the muted ink and the strong line were both darkened after it failed them.

Numbers are set in tabular figures so a column of counts aligns. Status is never carried by colour alone: every badge has a dot and a word. The sidebar is the one dark surface, which keeps the working area white and lets a status colour mean something. Components were lifted into the shared file once a second screen needed them, which is how the drawer, the numbered step list, the comparison pair and the oversized search field arrived.

refs.title: What was checked against what
body: Before each component was drawn, one search on Mobbin for the pattern, then two or three references read and reduced to what to take and what to leave. Recording the rejection matters as much as the reference: most of these products are for office workers with a mouse and a mailbox, and this one is for someone standing at a fryer.
Every row links to the screen on Mobbin.

modules.title: Quick Add: reporting from the floor
modules.finding: The form asked questions the reporter could not answer. Incident type came first, with options like first aid or lost time that nobody can predict while their hand is under the cold tap; the notifiable-to-the-regulator question sent people to a compliance matrix. Even area safety leads admitted asking the restaurant's safety champion which option to choose. Misclassified reports were sent back from above, and everyone learned that reporting was a way to get something wrong.
body: The redesign inverts the order. The reporter says what happened and how it happened, in the words they would use to a manager. Severity, classification and the regulator question move to the manager's review, after the welfare check, when the outcome is actually known. The safety team supported the inversion because it also gives them cleaner data.
Everything on the reporter's side is built for one thumb, mid-shift, on a personal phone, in a restaurant whose phone policy may not allow it. Nothing is asked that the system already knows.
modules.caption: The entry screen. One question, two answers, and the examples that resolve the only hesitation the research found. The old form opened on a dropdown of incident types.

states.title: Step 1, what happened
states.cap: Mechanisms, not classifications. Burn, cut, slip, lifting, chemical. The line above the list says the manager works out how serious it is later, so the reporter does not have to.

states.title: Step 2, with the error state
states.cap: Causes are filtered to the ones that fit a burn. The error names the field and offers the way out, because the old form's errors arrived days later from above.

states.title: Step 3, when and where
states.cap: Defaults to now and to the area the reporter is in, with a photo as an optional attachment rather than a required field.

states.title: Submitted
states.cap: A reference, a summary of what was sent, and four numbered steps saying what happens next. The last of them is the promise the old service broke: you are told what changed because you reported it.

states.title: The hazard path
states.cap: A condition, not an event. No injury questions, no severity, and the same closing promise.

states.title: The manager's review
states.cap: Where the classification lives. The welfare check comes first, then the outcome, then the regulator question, each answered by someone who now knows the answer.

steps.title: The hesitation is at the very start
steps.body: Team members stopped at the incident-versus-hazard choice, especially for a near miss. One entry point removes the first place people gave up, and the examples resolve the only hesitation the research found.
steps.quote: People reported to a person, not a platform. The barrier was the form, the phone and the threshold.
steps.rejected: Two forms with a chooser in front, which asks the reporter to classify before they have described anything.

steps.title: Mechanism first, outcome later
steps.body: What happened is the one thing the reporter knows for certain in the moment. Burn, cut, slip, written in the words people used in interviews rather than in the platform's taxonomy.
steps.quote: Nobody can predict whether it is first aid or lost time while their hand is under the cold tap.
steps.rejected: A fifteen-option incident-type dropdown, which is the field that came back corrected from above.

steps.title: Only the causes that fit
steps.body: Step two shows the causes that belong to the mechanism chosen at step one, so a burn never offers a vehicle cause. The error marks the question, not every answer.
steps.rejected: One long cause list for every mechanism, faster to build and slower to use.

steps.title: When and where, already filled in
steps.body: Both default to now and to the area the reporter is in, because reports are made standing up, mid-shift, on a personal phone. These are the only two required fields in the flow.
steps.quote: The cost people described was stepping off the floor during a rush.
steps.rejected: A free-text location field, which produced data nobody could group.

steps.title: The thing the old service never did
steps.body: The confirmation names what was sent and what happens next, and ends on the one thing reporters said they never got.
steps.quote: Minor reports were closed without a word, which built the belief that reporting does nothing for anyone else.
steps.rejected: A reference number and nothing else.

steps.title: A hazard is a condition, not an event
steps.body: The hazard path describes something that could cause harm and never asks about an injury. The old list mixed events in, so nobody knew which form to use.
steps.quote: \u201cThe floor is wet\u201d is a hazard. \u201cSomeone slipped\u201d is an incident.
steps.rejected: One combined form with conditional fields, which still opens on the question the reporter cannot answer.

steps.title: Classification belongs to whoever knows
steps.body: Severity is set by the manager from the treatment actually required, after the welfare check. The regulator question appears only when the outcome makes it relevant.
steps.quote: Managers have the context for cause; team members have the context for mechanism.
steps.rejected: Leaving severity with the reporter and correcting it later, which is what taught people that reporting was a way to get something wrong.

modules.title: Dashboard: the restaurant manager's shift
modules.finding: Location did not predict safety culture. The manager did. Where a manager talked about safety, thanked people for reports and showed the system on the first shift, reporting was strong regardless of where the restaurant was. That finding made the manager's screen the most important screen in the product.
body: So this dashboard is not a reporting console. It is a shift tool: what needs a person today, what is overdue, what was fixed and who reported it, and the routine that the research found to be the strongest lever. The vendor product opened on a permissions wall where the dashboard should have been.

The two charts answer the question the safety team could not answer from the platform's data: whether a quiet restaurant is a safe one. Hazards and incidents are plotted separately, because a restaurant finding hazards before they hurt anyone looks nothing like one that reports only after an injury.
modules.caption: The restaurant manager's dashboard at 1440 by 900. Four counts, a weekly trend read in a sentence, the open reports with the next human act as their status, and the loop closed on the right.

modules.title: Dashboard: the area manager, twelve restaurants
modules.finding: Reporting volume varied widely between restaurants and nobody could say why. Low volume could mean a safe restaurant or a silent one, and the existing lever was a reminder email that went to everyone and told no one anything.
body: The area view compares restaurants on the ratio of hazards to incidents rather than on report counts, and it names the three conversations worth having this week instead of sending twelve people the same message.

This is the screen where the study's central finding becomes an operating instrument: if the manager is the variable, the area manager's job is to find the managers who need a conversation, and to have it on evidence.
modules.caption: The area manager's dashboard. Twelve restaurants compared, three flagged, and the reasoning written next to the table rather than left to the reader.

states.title: One restaurant, opened
states.cap: Fourteen days of silence, what is open, the last three reports, and a note that starts a conversation rather than a reminder that starts nothing.

modules.title: Incidents and hazards: one register, two types
modules.finding: The platform's hazard categories contained events rather than conditions, so the two record types blurred at the point of entry and then had to be kept apart everywhere else. Reports also sat waiting because nothing said which ones needed a person today.
body: Incidents and hazards live in one register with one filter, because a manager's question is about their restaurant this week, not about a record type. The type is a column, not a navigation decision.
Status is written as the next human act. Welfare check due, action assigned, fixed and awaiting sign-off: each one names something a person does, so a list of statuses reads as a list of obligations.
modules.caption: The register with the quick filters that match the manager's questions, and the type as a column rather than a menu.

states.title: A row, opened
states.cap: The detail panel keeps the list in view, so a manager working through a morning's reports never loses their place.

states.title: Empty
states.cap: The empty state says what happened last rather than nothing at all, and names the person who was told.

modules.title: The incident record: welfare first, classification after
modules.finding: The old form asked for the outcome before the event. Severity and the regulatory question sat at the top, answered by a person who could not yet know, and corrected later by someone above them. People learned that reporting was a way to get something wrong.
body: The record puts the sequence back in the order the shift actually runs. What the reporter told us, then the welfare check, then the classification drawn from what happened, then the cause and the control, then the actions, then the person who reported it being told what changed.
The status pipeline across the top is the argument in one line: the record is not finished when it is logged, it is finished when someone has been told.
modules.caption: The incident record. The welfare check is the current step, and the classification below it is a manager's judgement recorded after the fact, not a reporter's guess recorded before it.

states.title: Closed
states.cap: Closing requires the loop to be closed: the record names what changed and who was told.

modules.title: Corrective actions: the half that was invisible
modules.finding: Reporters rarely heard what happened next. Minor reports were closed without a word, which built the belief that reporting helps you with a claim but does nothing for anyone else. The exception proved it: the restaurant where a faulty piece of equipment was fixed the same day had a story people kept telling.
body: Actions are the part of the service where a report turns into a change, and in the old workflow they were the part nobody outside the office could see. Here they are a board with owners and due dates, and closing one asks for evidence and offers to tell the person who reported it, with the message written for them.

The proposal rejected recognition programmes that reward report counts. The safety team's view was blunt: put an incentive on hazard reports and you get reports, not fewer hazards. So the artefact this module produces is a notice of outcomes, not a leaderboard.
modules.caption: The corrective actions board. Overdue is a state of the card, not a report someone runs, and the closed column is the one the monthly notice is printed from.

states.title: As a list
states.cap: The same actions as a table, for the manager who is checking due dates rather than moving work.

states.title: Closing an action
states.cap: Evidence, then the message to the reporter, on by default. Telling people is the system's behaviour, not somebody's good habit.

states.title: The monthly notice
states.cap: Generated from the closed actions and printed for the break room: what changed, who reported it, how long it took. It is the artefact the whole loop exists to produce, so it is annotated too.

modules.title: Emergency information: the screen nobody reads until they must
modules.finding: Emergency information was not the study's focus. The restaurant visits did look at the posters, the first-aid cabinet and the office setup, and the finding that carries over is the one about language: the people who need this are new, busy and do not know the terminology.
body: So the module is a picture of the restaurant rather than a list of records: where the extinguisher, the blanket, the eyewash and the spill kit actually are, with a legend in plain words and a date beside each check.

The right-hand column is the part used under pressure. Numbers big enough to read at arm's length, in the order you would need them, with the first-aider roster showing its own gap rather than hiding it.
modules.caption: Emergency information for one restaurant. The floor sketch is the record; the list beneath it is how the record gets checked.

states.title: The printable card
states.cap: The same content as one page for the wall, because the phone is in a locker in half the restaurants.

modules.title: Chemical register: an obligation that expires
modules.finding: Chemicals were outside the study's scope. The principle applied here is the one the research established everywhere else: the system should answer the question the person on shift actually has, in language they already use.
body: A safety data sheet is a compliance document with an expiry date, so the register leads with what is expiring and what is missing rather than with an alphabetical list of products.

The panel is written for the moment it is needed: what this is, what to wear, what to do if it goes on skin or in eyes, and the three steps for a spill. The regulatory document is attached underneath, not in front.
modules.caption: The chemical register. Status first, alphabet second, and PPE as a column so a new starter can read the requirement without opening anything.

states.title: A product, opened
states.cap: First aid in plain language above the data sheet, because the data sheet is not what anyone reads at the sink.

modules.title: Contractor management: the people the system forgets
modules.finding: Contractors were outside the study's scope. The finding that carries over is that managers work through the system on behalf of everyone else, and that open hazards were held in a record nobody on the floor could see.
body: Signing a contractor in is where an open hazard becomes useful to someone who has never been in the building: the sign-in reads the restaurant's open hazards and tells them, on the record, before they start.
Induction and insurance are dates that expire, so they are badges with a date on the row rather than a document someone has to open to find out.
modules.caption: Contractors. Who is on site now sits above the register, because that is the question a manager is asked, not who is on the list.

states.title: Signing someone in
states.cap: The hazards they are told about are filled in from the restaurant's open reports, so the briefing is a record rather than a memory.

modules.title: Knowledge base: the threshold question, answered
modules.finding: The barrier was not fear. Team members trusted their managers and nobody described feeling embarrassed to report, even when they had been doing the wrong thing. The barrier was the form, the phone and the threshold: not knowing whether a thing counted. A plain-language guide to what counts was one of the concept mockups delivered in December 2025.
body: So the knowledge base opens on the question people actually type, and its first article is the one that unblocks reporting: incident or hazard, with examples from a restaurant rather than definitions from a standard.

The answer to not being sure is written into the article and matches the promise the reporting flow makes: report it as whatever it looks like to you, and the manager sorts out the classification from what happened.
modules.caption: The knowledge base. Search first, then the article that resolves the threshold question, with the examples in the words people used in interviews.

states.title: Searching
states.cap: Results are articles and actions together, so the answer to a hazard question can be to report the hazard.
